13.1: 13.1 Charity. From this place the Apostle instructs morally, as if to say: Because charity is to be had, let it abide in you, and forget not hospitality. For by this some have been hidden, like Lot not knowing they were angels, yet knowing who was in them.
13.3: 13.3 As if bound with them, that is, as you would wish yourselves, if bound, to be helped, or those who labor.
13.5: 13.5 Let your manners be. After the Hebrews had lost their goods, they wished to gather them again: which the Apostle forbids. But lest they say: What if necessities fail? he adds consolation. Without covetousness. The covetous is he who is tenacious in giving, greedy in receiving. I will not leave you. God says this to everyone hoping in him, as to Joshua, so he is with us, that we may say confidently, etc. Nor forsake you. He would be forsaken who died of hunger: but because this is not so, let not man be covetous.
13.6: 13.6 I will not fear, etc. Every adversary man, even the devil, who is man by office, in that he deceives man.
13.7: 13.7 Remember, etc. Because it is long to speak of each, he admonishes to follow the masters.
13.8: 13.8 Jesus Christ, etc. This pertains to the preceding sentence, where he testified that God had said: I will not leave you, nor forsake you. It might have seemed to them that this promise belonged to Joshua only, to which he answers that he will help us as he helped him. As if: There is no doubt, because he who yesterday, that is in the past, helped Joshua, today, that is in the present, helps, and will help those to come through all ages.
13.10: 13.10 We have an altar, etc. Food is not to be studied, because we have an altar, that is the body of Christ, in the faith of which offered prayers and works are acceptable to God, of which they have no right to eat, etc. The tabernacle, etc. That is, the observances of the law, so that those who distinguish meats and keep other legal things of this kind, which he signifies by the name of tabernacle, because they were imposed for a time; or, our body is rightly called a tabernacle, because we must stay in it for a time, and therefore it is not to be served in its desires.
13.11: 13.11 For the bodies of those beasts, etc. By a double allegory, of which one is of the Old and the other of the New Testament, he proves that the body of Christ is not to be eaten by those who serve the tabernacle. For to this end the bodies of animals are burned outside the camp, and therefore Christ suffered outside the gate, that we, who wish to be cleansed from sins by his body and blood, about to suffer reproaches and straits, may forsake the delights of the tabernacle. Of animals. Christ was signified by those animals.
13.12: 13.12 The gate. The gate of the city is the sense of the body, in none of which Christ sinned: and therefore he suffered outside. And let us, the door of the senses being closed to vices, suffer outside.
13.15: 13.15 By him therefore. Who is the way for us, from whom we take example, let us run to martyrdom. Of the confident. AUGUSTINE. You then who fear the Lord, praise him, etc., down to of which invisible sacrifice that visible sacred rite was the sign.
13.16: 13.16 Of doing good. The opinion of the wicked about gluttony having been made void, he returns to morals. Of doing good, that is, of liberality toward others. And if your substance be taken away, yet from what you have give alms. This he had said above: Not leaving the collection.
13.17: 13.17 That with joy. Let us do these things surely with joy, when we see men advancing in the words of God. For then the laborer labors with joy in the fields, when he attends to the trees and sees fruit; when he attends to the crop and sees abundance. Then he understands that he has not labored without cause, not without cause bent his back, not without cause worn his hands, not without cause borne cold and heat. It is not expedient for you. I do not say: it is not expedient for them, because it also profits them to be saddened for you. For those superiors, when they are made sad over your evils, the sadness itself is expedient for them, but not for you. Likewise therefore in the Lord's field let us work good, prelates and subjects, that we may likewise rejoice over the reward.
13.18: 13.18 Pray for us. He strikes the pride and elation of mind of certain pontiffs, who disdain to ask their subjects to pour out prayers for them. We have a good conscience, that is, conscience does not accuse us, nor are we conscious that we have laid snares for you, brought forth nothing with feigning, done nothing for the sake of trafficking. Think not therefore anything sinister. In all things. The Apostle was accused of neglecting his own nation, but he shows that he has affection toward all Jews and Gentiles, in whose past good he rejoices, and wishes better things for them in the future.
13.21: 13.21 Doing in you, etc. For you can have nothing good unless he go before and follow.
13.22: 13.22 For I have written to you in few words, etc. As if: No one can refuse length of discourse, for this was what the adversaries did, and therefore he touches it covertly. Salute all your superiors. As he writes generally to all, so he wishes salvation generally to all prelates and subjects. To salute is to wish salvation.
